questions.prompt: Classifying the stationary points of a smooth function starts by
options: solving the equation that sets the gradient equal to zero
replacing the function by its absolute value
questions.explanation: A stationary point is defined by a zero gradient, so the list of candidates is the solution set of that equation. Compactness is an existence tool and does not locate the point. Integration recovers a function from a derivative and is not the classification. The absolute value creates new corners and a different function.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 4y\). What is the value at the stationary point?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \((2x - 2,\ 2y - 4)\), so the only stationary point is \((1, 2)\). The value is \(1 + 4 - 2 - 8 = -5\). Completing the square gives \((x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 - 5\), which shows the same point is the unique global minimizer. Reporting 1 or 2 gives a coordinate. Reporting 5 drops the sign. Reporting \(-4\) is the linear coefficient on \(y\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: An indefinite Hessian at a stationary point means the point is
questions.explanation: Indefinite means one positive eigenvalue and one negative eigenvalue. The function rises along the first eigenvector and falls along the second, which is a saddle. A local minimizer would need every eigenvalue nonnegative, and a local maximizer would need every eigenvalue nonpositive. The gradient was already set to zero before the Hessian was read, so the point is stationary.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to classify stationary points and then test a global claim.
questions.explanation: The candidates are the solutions of the gradient equation, and the list has to be complete before a comparison of values means anything. The Hessian eigenvalues then separate local minima, local maxima, and saddles, with a zero eigenvalue left undecided. A local minimizer becomes global only after a separate argument: the function is coercive, a sublevel set is compact, or every other stationary value is worse and no direction runs off to \(-\infty\). Comparing values before the list is complete can miss a lower stationary point.

steps: Compute the gradient and set it equal to zero.
Solve for every real stationary point.
Classify each one from the eigenvalues of its Hessian.
Use the values, or coercivity, before calling one of them a global minimizer.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^3 + y^3 - 3x - 3y\). Which statements hold?
questions.explanation:
The gradient vanishes when \(x^2 = 1\) and \(y^2 = 1\), so the four points have coordinates \(\pm 1\). The Hessian is \(\operatorname{diag}(6x, 6y)\).
• At \((1, 1)\) both eigenvalues are positive, so the point is a strict local minimizer. The value is \(-4\).
• At \((1, -1)\) and at \((-1, 1)\) the eigenvalues have opposite signs, so both points are saddles.
• At \((-1, -1)\) both eigenvalues are negative, so the point is a strict local maximizer, not a minimizer.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = t^4 - 8t^2\). What is the global minimum value?
questions.explanation: The derivative is \(4t^3 - 16t = 4t(t - 2)(t + 2)\), so the stationary points are \(t = 0\) and \(t = \pm 2\). The values are \(0\) and \(16 - 32 = -16\). The second derivative \(12t^2 - 16\) is negative at the origin and positive at \(\pm 2\), so the origin is a local maximizer and the other two points are local minimizers. The fourth power dominates at infinity, so \(-16\) is the global minimum, attained twice. Reporting \(-8\) uses the coefficient. Reporting 0 is the local maximum value. Reporting 2 is a location.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: For \(a \ne 0\), the stationary point of \(\tfrac12 a x^2 + b x + \tfrac12 c y^2 + d y\) has first coordinate \(-b/a\) when \(c \ne 0\) as well. Write that first coordinate as an expression in a and b.
questions.explanation:
The partial derivative in \(x\) is \(a x + b\), and it vanishes at \(x = -b/a\). The partial derivative in \(y\) does not enter that coordinate.
• \(b/a\) misses the sign.
• \(-a/b\) inverts the ratio.
• \(-b\) drops the curvature \(a\).

questions.prompt: A note claims that the origin is a local minimizer of \(f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2\). Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: The gradient really does vanish, the Hessian really is \(\operatorname{diag}(2, -2)\), and a local minimizer really does need a positive semidefinite Hessian. The false step is the semidefinite claim. A negative diagonal entry is a negative eigenvalue, so the Hessian is indefinite and the origin is a saddle.

steps: Both partial derivatives vanish at the origin.
The Hessian at the origin is diagonal with entries 2 and -2.
A diagonal Hessian with both a positive entry and a negative entry is positive semidefinite.
Positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian is necessary at an interior local minimizer.
reasons: A negative diagonal entry means the Hessian is not positive semidefinite.
The partial derivatives do not vanish at the origin.
An interior local minimizer can have an indefinite Hessian.

questions.prompt: For \(f(x, y) = x^2 + y^4\), the origin is stationary and the Hessian there is singular. The right reading is that
options: the origin is a saddle because of the zero eigenvalue
the origin is a local maximizer
the Hessian test is silent, and nonnegativity of \(f\) shows that the origin is a global minimizer
questions.explanation: The gradient is \((2x,\ 4y^3)\), which vanishes only at the origin. The Hessian there is \(\operatorname{diag}(2, 0)\), so the sufficient test does not fire and the zero eigenvalue is not a saddle by itself. The function is a sum of even powers, hence nonnegative, and it equals zero only at the origin. That is a strict global minimizer found without the sufficient test. It is not a maximizer.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 8y\). What is the value at the stationary point?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \((2x - 6,\ 2y + 8)\), so the stationary point is \((3, -4)\). The value is \(9 + 16 - 18 - 32 = -25\). Completing the square gives \((x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 - 25\), and the Hessian is twice the identity, so the point is the unique strict global minimizer. Reporting 3 or \(-4\) gives a coordinate. Reporting 25 drops the sign. Reporting \(-6\) is a linear coefficient.

questions.prompt: A minimizer on a smooth equality constraint
options: must be a stationary point of the objective alone
can have a nonzero objective gradient
must have an indefinite Hessian of the objective
questions.explanation: The constraint removes the ambient interior, so the objective gradient need not vanish. It has to be normal to the constraint surface. A nonzero objective gradient is therefore compatible with optimality. The Hessian of the objective alone is not required to be indefinite. Strictness is still possible along the surface.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2 + 2x\). Which statements hold?
options: The function has no local minimizer.
questions.explanation:
The gradient is \((2x + 2,\ -2y)\), so the only stationary point is \((-1, 0)\). The Hessian is \(\operatorname{diag}(2, -2)\), which is indefinite, so the point is a saddle and neither a local minimizer nor a local maximizer.
On the open plane every local minimizer of a differentiable function is stationary. The only candidate is a saddle, and \(f\) goes to \(-\infty\) as \(\lvert y \rvert\) grows, so no local minimizer exists.
